business-narrative.name: Business Narrative
business-narrative.summary: Tell a business strategy or solution as a story: setting, challenge, tension, hero, plan, outcome. Useful for internal alignment decks, town halls, and any audience that responds better to story shape than to bullet lists.

beats.name: Introduction
beats.description: Engage the audience and set expectations for the next twenty minutes. Tell them you're going to tell them a story — and then start telling it. Avoid a separate agenda slide; the introduction is the first scene.

beats.name: Setting
beats.description: Establish the world the story takes place in: the team, the market, the moment. Just enough context that the challenge will feel meaningful when it arrives.

beats.name: Challenge
beats.description: Identify the issue at hand. Concrete, specific, attributable. The challenge is the inciting incident — the thing that pulled the rest of the story into motion.

beats.name: Tension
beats.description: Raise the stakes. What happens if the challenge isn't met? Quantify the cost, name the people affected, surface the trade-offs that make the choice hard. Tension is what makes the audience lean in.

beats.name: Solution
beats.description: Reveal the strategy or hero of the story. Lead with what changes for the audience or customer when the solution is in place. This is the turn from problem to promise.

beats.name: Implementation
beats.description: Describe the path to success. Phases, owners, milestones, key bets. Show the audience that the solution has weight behind it — not just intent.

beats.name: Recap
beats.description: Bring the audience back to the surface with a clear summary of what was said and decided. Echo the language from the opening so the story feels closed.

beats.name: Conclusion
beats.description: Reinforce the key message and the call to action. End on the line you most want repeated in tomorrow's hallway conversations.
beats.instructions: Reinforce takeaways and call to action

all-hands.name: All Hands
all-hands.summary: The full company — mixed roles, mixed seniority, looking for context, signal, and inclusion.
all-hands.description: An all-hands audience spans the whole company. Frame the period in terms anyone can grasp: what we did, what mattered, and what's next. Highlight people and teams; surface successes and challenges; close on a forward-looking note. Avoid lapsing into function-specific jargon.

decide.name: Drive a Decision
decide.summary: Frame options, evidence, tradeoffs, and a recommendation so the audience can choose.
decide.description: Use when the deck exists to get a yes/no, select among options, approve a recommendation, or resolve ambiguity. Lead with the decision needed and make the ask explicit.
decide.outcome: The audience makes or authorizes a clear decision.

casual.name: Casual
casual.summary: Warm, plain-spoken voice for internal updates and customer storytelling.
casual.description: Friendly and direct. Use first- and second-person freely; favor short sentences and contractions. Numbers are still welcome — they just sit alongside human-scale framing rather than leading.
voiceCues: Favor short sentences and active voice.
Frame metrics with a human-scale anchor when possible.
samplePhrases: We shipped the new dashboard last week, and customers are already moving over.
Here's where we ended up on hiring this quarter.
It's been a busy month — here's the recap.

classic.name: Classic
classic.description: A timeless, clean, and versatile theme with balanced color contrasts and classic typography. Ideal for professional, readable presentations.

bold-red.name: Bold Red
bold-red.summary: Confident red and teal accents for urgent, high-salience stories.
bold-red.description: A bold red-led scheme with teal and navy support. Use it when the deck needs urgency, contrast, and clear emphasis.

cool-horizon.name: Cool Horizon
cool-horizon.summary: Cool blue-green palette tuned for professional business decks.
cool-horizon.description: A balanced cool-toned scheme with deep navy, business blues, and teal accents. It works well across strategy, finance, and technical narratives.

aparajita.name: Aparajita
aparajita.description: Aparajita is a sans serif OPF font scheme for complex script presentations, using Aparajita for both headings and body text.

tenorite.name: Tenorite
tenorite.description: Tenorite is a sans serif OPF font scheme for Latin presentations, using Tenorite Display for headings with Tenorite for body text.

title.name: Title
title.summary: Reach for it when the slide is a single headline: a cover, a divider or a one-line statement.
title.description: A title and nothing else. The slide carries one headline with no subtitle or body, so the message is the whole slide.

text-2x.name: Text 2x
text-2x.summary: Reach for it when two blocks of prose sit side by side, such as a before and an after or a pro and a con.
text-2x.description: A title above two text blocks in a row. Use it to pair two explanations, set a problem next to its answer, or compare two options in sentences.

chart-2x.name: Chart 2x
chart-2x.summary: Reach for it when two charts are read together, each with its own note.
chart-2x.description: A title above two charts, each followed by a text block, in two columns. Use it to compare two series, two periods or two segments side by side.

list-2x.name: List 2x
list-2x.summary: Reach for it when two lists contrast or complement each other, such as pros and cons.
list-2x.description: A title above two lists side by side. Use it for two categories of equal weight, such as strengths and risks, or what is in scope and what is not.
